extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature and drama; subscribers and members of the Augustan Reprint Society
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-evaluative guidance for assessing Shakespeare's dramatic works (style, characterization, plot, diction, imagination) together with procedural/selection notes for a scholarly reprint society's publications and membership terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively, vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: His Images are indeed ev'ry where so lively, that the Thing he would represent stands full before you, and you possess ev'ry Part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the image of Patience in a monument ('She pin'd in Thought, / And sate like Patience on a Monument, Smiling at Grief.'). Note: powerful, uncommon images that make passions visible are marks of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization appropriate to persons (manners and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manners of his Characters, in Acting or Speaking what is proper for them, and fit to be shown by the Poet, he may be generally justify'd, and in very many places greatly commended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Characters should act and speak fittingly for their social rank and situation; examples praised: Falstaff, Shylock, Prospero, Jacques. Consistent sustaining of character across scenes (Falstaff across three plays) is commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original invention and imaginative flights
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatness of this Author's Genius do's no where so much appear, as where he gives his Imagination an entire Loose, and raises his Fancy to a flight above Mankind and the Limits of the visible World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Tempest, Midsummer-Night's Dream, Macbeth, Hamlet; invention of new characters and 'a new manner of Language' (Caliban). Originality of incidents and imaginative scope are high virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural, easy style suited to characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stile of his Comedy is, in general, Natural to the Characters, and easie in it self; and the Wit most commonly sprightly and pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forced learnedness where natural diction serves better. Naturalness is preferred even when classical polish is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and grandeur of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: His Sentiments and Images of Things are Great and Natural; and his Expression (tho' perhaps in some Instances a little Irregular) just, and rais'd in Proportion to his Subject and Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should rise in proportion to subject; occasional irregularities tolerated when overall expression is manly and proper. Example: 'the Diction manly and proper' in Othello.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-specific language and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: That extravagant Character of Caliban is mighty well sustain'd, shews a wonderful Invention in the Author, who could strike out such a particular wild Image, and is certainly one of the finest and most uncommon Grotesques that was ever seen. That Shakespear had ... devis'd and adapted a new manner of Language for that Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language must suit the character's nature — invent or adapt language for nonstandard or fantastical characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic humour and variety of humours
rubrics_metrics.description: There is certainly a great deal of Entertainment in his Comical Humours; ... there is a pleasing and a well-distinguish'd Variety in those Characters which he thought fit to meddle with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the diversity and sustained amusement of comic characters (examples: Falstaff, Malvolio, Parolles). Beware of making vicious characters too agreeable without consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced depiction of vices and virtues to evoke pity/compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: He has shewn him Tyrannical, Cruel, and Insolent in his Prosperity; and yet, by a wonderful Address, he makes his Fall and Ruin the Subject of general Compassion. The whole Man, with his Vices and Virtues, is finely and exactly describ'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tragic characterization renders both faults and humanity to move audience pity (example: Cardinal Wolsey). Avoid one-sided portrayal that denies complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Terror and Horror (stage propriety)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is to distinguish rightly between Horror and Terror. The latter is a proper Passion of Tragedy, but the former ought always to be carefully avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Tragedy should aim to raise terror (acceptable passion) but avoid depicting barbarous actions or horror onstage that offend decorum (example contrast with Electra/Orestes parricide). Use restraint in representation of extreme acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility/probability of incidents (suspension of disbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tale indeed, in that Part relating to the Caskets, and the extravagant and unusual kind of Bond given by Antonio, is a little too much remov'd from the Rules of Probability: But taking the Fact for granted, we must allow it to be very beautifully written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While poetic beauty can excuse improbability, excessive departures from probability weaken a fable; judge whether language/character compensates for unlikely incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable (plot) arrangement, order and conduct of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fable is what is generally plac'd the first, among those that are reckon'd the constituent Parts of a Tragick or Heroick Poem; ... with the Fable ought to be consider'd, the fit Disposition, Order and Conduct of its several Parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate completeness and ordering of the plot (disposition, order, conduct). Johnson notes Shakespeare often followed original tales and did not always invent fables — this affects assessments of structural design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and spatial coherence (scene/time extent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all his Historical Plays comprehend a great length of Time, and very different and distinct Places: And in his Antony and Cleopatra, the Scene travels over the greatest Part of the Roman Empire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether jumps in time/place serve the drama or produce carelessness; long spans and many settings are acceptable if they aid characterization and narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and adaptation of historical or classical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: For the two last especially, you find 'em exactly as they are describ'd by Plutarch, from whom certainly Shakespear copy'd 'em. He has indeed follow'd his Original pretty close, and taken in several little Incidents that might have been spar'd in a Play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity and creative adaptation of source materials (Plutarch, novels, romances). Faithful adaptation that preserves character can be praise-worthy even when it includes incidental material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observance (or deliberate departure) of classical unities
rubrics_metrics.description: If one undertook to examine the greatest part of these by those Rules which are establish'd by Aristotle ... it would be no very hard Task to find a great many Faults: But as Shakespear liv'd under a kind of mere Light of Nature, and had never been made acquainted with the Regularity of those written Precepts, so it would be hard to judge him by a Law he knew nothing of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity (time/place/action) matters in classical theory but departures are defensible when natural genius and the needs of English drama make different choices (The Tempest is noted as unusually exact in unities). Judge in context of authorial aims and historical stage practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of revision and careful editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Praise of seldom altering or blotting out what he writ, which was given him by the Players who were the first Publishers of his Works after his Death, was what Johnson could not bear; he thought it impossible ... to reach those Excellencies of Poetry with the Ease of a first Imagination, which himself with infinite Labour and Study could but hardly attain to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard: careful revision and pruning are valued; an author who never blots may produce faults that careful editing would remove. Consider evidence of sloppiness or lapses that revision could have fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive wordplay and doggerel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stile of his Comedy is ... sprightly and pleasing, except in those places where he runs into Dogrel Rhymes, as in The Comedy of Errors, and a Passage or two in some other Plays. As for his Jingling sometimes, and playing upon Words, it was the common Vice of the Age he liv'd in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit and wordplay are virtues when tasteful; excessive jingling, doggerel, or cheap verbal tricks are faults (though partly historically contextualized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to move audiences (emotional force)
rubrics_metrics.description: No Dramatick Writer ever succeeded better in raising Terror in the Minds of an Audience than Shakespear has done. ... both shew how powerful he was, in giving the strongest Motions to our Souls that they are capable of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a play by its ability to stir profound emotions (terror, pity, tenderness). Praised examples: Macbeth, Hamlet, scenes of murder and remorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for performance and actorly comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man ... must have made his way into the Esteem of all Men of Letters, by this only Excellency. No Man is better acquainted with Shakespear's manner of Expression, and indeed he has study'd him so well, and is so much a Master of him, that whatever Part of his he performs he does it as if it had been written on purpose for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether text yields clear roles for actors and whether performances enhance the play's virtues (Betterton's Hamlet is offered as evidence of performance-shaped quality). Consider performability and how well passages function onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of genre-blending (trage-comedy) to audience taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Those which are called Histories, and even some of his Comedies, are really Tragedies, with a run or mixture of Comedy amongst 'em. That way of Trage-Comedy was the common Mistake of that Age, and is indeed become so agreeable to the English Tast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether mixture of tragic and comic elements works for the intended audience; the English taste accepted such blends though some critics dislike them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of learning vs natural genius (scholarship vs instinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson was certainly a very good Scholar, and in that had the advantage of Shakespear; tho' at the same time I believe it must be allow'd, that what Nature gave the latter, was more than a Ballance for what Books had given the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: consider whether learned borrowing or raw natural genius better serves poetic ends. Lack of classical scholarship need not be a fatal fault if natural powers compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection policy for reprint publications (series grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: At least two items will be printed from each of the three following groups. Series IV: Men, Manners, and Critics; Series V: Drama; Series VI: Poetry and Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural rule for the Augustan Reprint Society's output: ensure representation from each thematic group; examples of planned titles for each series are listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues will appear, as usual, in May, July, September, November, January, and March.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular bimonthly (six issues per year) schedule — plan production and mailing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership fees, eligibility, and pricing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership fees will be kept at the present annual rate of $2.50 in the United States and Canada, $2.75 in Great Britain and the continent. Libraries as well as individuals are eligible for membership. Since the publications are issued without profit, however, no discount can be allowed to libraries, agents, or booksellers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative constraints: fixed low fees, no institutional discounts, publications non-profit; new members may obtain a complete run of the first year's publications for $2.50.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended audience for the reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Students, scholars, and bibliographers of literature, history, and philology will find the publications valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target acquisitions and marketing to academic libraries and individual scholars; encourage subscribers to ensure college libraries receive mailings.
